stances.claim: CJ Peralta's 10-point program is well-conceived but Peralta would be acclaimed even for just achieving its first goal -- elimination of SC and lower-court backlog -- because that single achievement addresses the festering core of speedy-justice failure.
stances.rhetorical_move: single-goal-as-legacy framing (collapsing a 10-point program into one acclaim-conferring achievement)

stances.claim: The 2016 SC stats -- 6,526 new cases received but only 1,028 decided (a 6:1 ratio) -- and a 14,491-case docket are a damning failure of institutional output, with each of 15 justices carrying ~966 old cases plus 400 new ones.

His own 'Operation Zero Backlog' -- a judicial bayanihan with voluntary pool-pickup and footnote disclosure to protect ponente reputation -- worked, reducing the backlog to about 200 by his retirement; it was a viable model that was abandoned.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-precedent vindication (his model worked when followed)

stances.claim: The July 31, 2007 successor plan was viable in design ('in my humble opinion') but failed because it was promulgated 'not for release,' meaning incoming justices never learned of it, and retiring justices left their backlogs uncleared.
stances.rhetorical_move: design-versus-implementation diagnosis (the plan didn't fail, its execution did)

stances.claim: What Peralta needs is not another plan but a doable and transparent one that rallies the full cooperation of his colleagues -- implying the missing ingredient is collective commitment, not procedural design.

notable_anecdotes: The 'judicial bayanihan' coinage -- CJ's framing of Operation Zero Backlog as a Filipino communal labor tradition transposed into the SC, with light-load justices voluntarily picking cases from a common pool, and the footnote disclosure protecting the ponente from the laggard charge.
The '6:1 ratio' arithmetic: 6,526 cases in vs 1,028 decided in 2016 -- used as a one-line indictment of post-2006 SC output.

Estelito P. Mendoza's 12/5/2019 letter on Republic v. Lucio C. Tan -- a 'super lawyer' writing publicly to invoke the constitutional 24-month deadline, used by CJ as evidence that the backlog problem is now drawing complaint from the bar's top echelon.
The 'not for release' designation on the 2007 plan -- CJ's quiet diagnosis that the procedural secrecy itself caused the succession-ignorance that doomed implementation.
Panganiban-era figure: backlog reduced to ~200 cases by Dec 7, 2006 -- offered as living proof that institutional backlog is tractable.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens 2020 endorsing CJ Diosdado Peralta's 10-point program and arguing that Peralta would be acclaimed for achieving just the first goal -- elimination of SC and lower-court backlog. He uses 2016 stats from Gio-Samar v. DOTC to indict post-2006 institutional output: 6,526 new cases received but only 1,028 decided (a 6:1 ratio), leaving a 14,491-case docket and giving each of 15 justices an average load of ~966 old cases plus ~400 new ones a year. He revisits his own term's 'Operation Zero Backlog,' a judicial 'bayanihan' in which light-load justices voluntarily picked cases from a shared pool, with a footnote disclosing the pool-pickup to protect the ponente from the laggard charge; by his retirement on Dec 7, 2006, the backlog had fallen to ~200. The successor plan -- the formal July 31, 2007 'Internal Policy to Achieve and Maintain a Zero Backlog' -- was, 'in my humble opinion,' viable in design but failed in implementation: promulgated 'not for release,' it never reached the incoming justices, and retiring justices simply left their backlogs to successors who did not even know the plan existed. By 2016 the docket had ballooned from 8,741 (Jan 2007) to 14,491. Now even super lawyer Estelito P. Mendoza has written CJ Peralta complaining that Republic v. Lucio C. Tan (GR 203592) remains unresolved in violation of the constitutional deadline. Panganiban -- speaking as a former CJ himself -- supports Peralta's effort and prescribes the missing ingredient: a 'doable and transparent' plan that rallies full collegial cooperation, not just procedural design.
